keyFindings.description: The recreated-bucket branch of summarizer.pass (drop the queue and the held set when takeChanges reports a reset) has no test. With the branch removed, GOWORK=off go test -count=1 ./internal/cistore/ passes (reproduced by the reviewer; the tester saw the same, and saw envoy_ci_legacy_records_held stay 2 -> 2 -> 3 on the real binary where head goes 2 -> 0 -> 1). Add a test that fails without the branch: held records and a queued record in the old bucket, the bucket recreated, then the held count counts only the new bucket's records and the old queued key is not attempted.

'rather than being published again at the pass on every tick' is garbled and false: passes no longer run on every tick. Use the markOverflowed comment's wording (cistore.go:822-823), e.g. 'rather than being published again at every attempt'.
Dead branch: settle is called only with the record schedule judged verdictAttempt at the same now, and schedule returns that only when claimFresh is false. Delete the claimFresh check in settle.

heldBack has no production caller left; its only caller is the test oracle at summary_loop_test.go:25. Move it into the test file and point the '(heldBack)' comments in loop.go (102, 134, 143, 249) at legacyBacklog / verdictHeld.

testSummarizers never forgets a store: every store runSummaryTick touched (the benchmark's 12,000- and 30,000-record stores included) stays in memory and attached until the test binary exits, and a later StartSummaryLoop on such a store panics naming the attach, not the helper. Have openStore register a t.Cleanup that drops the entry and detaches.

notDefects: summarizer.mu: it makes a summarizer safe for runSummaryTick's use from tests and costs nothing measurable; removing it is a style choice.
cacheReset flag vs marking every cached key at reset: same result; the explicit flag is clearer.
A change marked during a pass that overran a grid instant with an empty queue waits one more tick: needs a >1 s pass with no attempt.
gridIndexAtOrAfter overflows only for deadlines ~292 years ahead; the timestamps come from the listener's own clock.
